# Psalm 18:1–25: Research notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**What I couldn't find:** I ran out of searches before finding any Catholic or Orthodox pages (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), any netbible.org notes, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material on this psalm. Those categories are left out. Where I've labelled a writer's tradition, the label comes from the site (StudyLight tags Gill and Clarke). The Reformed label for Calvin is the standard description and isn't stated on the page.

---

## Title and verses 1–3

**Title:**
- Guzik says this is one of the longest psalms and has one of the longest titles. He thinks it was written after Saul's death and the years before David became king. He notes that Saul is mentioned separately from "all his enemies," which he reads as a sign of David's undeserved kindness to Saul. The song is nearly the same as 2 Samuel 22. Guzik suggests David wrote it young and sang it again in old age. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- The Pulpit Commentary dates it after the victories of 2 Samuel 10 and before the Bathsheba events of 2 Samuel 11–12. It points out that the psalm shows no remorse for any particular sin. It thinks the psalm was probably written for a great public thanksgiving. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 1: "I love You, O LORD":**
- Guzik says the Hebrew word for "love" is unusual, emotional and tender. He cites Boice, Trapp and Maclaren. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- Spurgeon calls it "intensely forcible," a love of the deepest kind. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps018.cfm
- Pulpit says that elsewhere this verb only describes God's love for people, never people's love for God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Bible.org (Utley) agrees the word is related to "womb," but warns against reading too much into that, since the same root also means "vulture." Meaning should come from context. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-18
- A Puritan writer quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury* says that just as God's love starts all our blessings, our love for God should be what they produce. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps018.cfm

**v. 2: the names for God:**
- Guzik counts nine titles. He says a rock gave shade, shelter in its cracks, and firm footing in a fight. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- Pulpit says "Rock" (*sela*) is the word often used of Petra, and "horn" stands for strength and dignity (compare Luke 1:69). It quotes Delitzsch's count of seven names, a number standing for completeness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Utley notes that two different Hebrew words are translated "rock." "Horn" means power, but it might also mean "hill," which would fit with "fortress." https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-18
- Spurgeon says the repeated "rock" isn't needless repetition. The first is a rock to hide in, the second a rock of firmness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps018.cfm

**v. 3:**
- Pulpit reads the verb as ongoing: "I call, and will always call." David is safe for as long as he keeps calling. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Guzik points out that David once despaired of escaping Saul (1 Samuel 27:1). He quotes Spurgeon: "To be saved singing is to be saved indeed." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/

## Verses 4–6: the danger and the cry

**v. 4:**
- Pulpit pictures death as a hunter with nets and cords. It links the verse to the years Saul hunted David, and takes "torrents of Belial" to mean crowds of Saul's men blocking his escape. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Barnes says "Belial" basically means worthless, and so wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-4.html
- Ellicott thinks the wording in 2 Samuel ("waves of death") is probably the original, and links Hebrew fear of floods to stories like the Flood and the Red Sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-4.htm
- Gill applies the floods of ungodly men to Herod, Pilate and the others who gathered against Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-4.html

**v. 5:**
- Pulpit: death and Sheol (the grave) are pictured as hunters closing their nets. "Confronted me" means "took me by surprise." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Guzik takes Sheol here simply as the grave or death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/

**v. 6:**
- Guzik says the "temple" must be God's heavenly temple, because Solomon's temple hadn't been built yet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- Pulpit suggests the tabernacle or heaven. It notes that the word for "cry" is the same one used for Israel's cry in Egypt (Exodus 2:23). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Matthew Henry: David prayed and God heard, and if we pray as he did we will succeed as he did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-10.htm

## Verses 7–15: God comes down in the storm

**Literal or poetic? (vv. 7–15)** This is the main interpretive question in this section.
- Pulpit says the passage shouldn't be taken literally. It is poetry describing how David's enemies were thrown into confusion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Guzik says the images draw on the Exodus, Sinai and the conquest of Canaan. He adds that David may also have actually seen storms like this during years of his life the Bible doesn't record. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- Matthew Henry says these words can't be applied to David's own history, and that "a greater than David is here." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-10.htm

**v. 7:**
- Pulpit: God's anger at David's enemies causes all the upheaval. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Guzik quotes Horne: when a king goes to war, his whole kingdom is stirred up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/

**v. 8:**
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) calls smoke from the nostrils a Middle Eastern way of describing fierce anger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- Pulpit notes that the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "in his anger" instead. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 9:**
- Pulpit: in a storm the clouds really do seem to come down. God "comes down" whenever he rescues the oppressed. It compares the thick darkness at Sinai. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Matthew Henry says God didn't send an angel but came himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_018.cfm

**v. 10: riding a cherub:**
- Pulpit says the image is beyond experience. God is carried by the highest creatures, the cherubim. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Calvin says it teaches that angels direct even the force of the winds, and he sees a reference to the ark of the covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-10.html
- Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist) describes the storm as God's chariot, driven by the ministry of angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-10.html
- Barnes, by contrast, says the cherubim are an imagined picture of God's majesty, not real beings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-10.htm
- Gill (labelled Baptist) suggests the cherubim may stand for gospel ministers taking the message to the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-10.htm
- Poole and Guzik stress how fast God came to help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/

**v. 11:**
- Pulpit: God hid himself in the clouds. His actions are always hidden and beyond our understanding. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**vv. 12–13:**
- Pulpit: the brightness is lightning breaking through the clouds. The hail mixed with fire recalls the plague in Egypt. Thunder is God's voice, and the phrase "hail and coals of fire" is repeated for emphasis. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 14:**
- Pulpit: God's "arrows" can mean any sharp pain, of body or mind, that he sends. The storm scatters the enemy, as at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:24). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Matthew Henry: the arrows are lightning, and they always hit their target. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_018.cfm

**v. 15:**
- Pulpit: lightning lights up the riverbeds while the earthquake splits the ground open. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

## Verses 16–19: rescued and set free

**v. 16:**
- Pulpit and Gill note that the verb "drew me out" appears elsewhere only in Exodus 2:10, when Moses was drawn out of the Nile. This suggests a parallel between Moses and David. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-16.html
- Barnes: water often stands for trouble and disaster. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-16.htm
- In a sermon, Spurgeon warns that we shouldn't expect miraculous rescues like this to be repeated literally. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-16.html

**v. 17:**
- Pulpit: the "strong enemy" is usually taken to be Saul. His courtiers had no power once he was gone. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 18:**
- Keil & Delitzsch say God became the staff the homeless fugitive leaned on. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-18.htm

**v. 19: "because He delighted in me":**
- Pulpit: the "large place" is open ground without traps. "Delighted in me" sums up the reasons God favoured David, which vv. 20–26 then explain. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Guzik reads it two ways: God chose and anointed David, and God was also pleased with how David lived. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/
- Keil & Delitzsch connect it to God's grace in choosing David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-17.htm

**Christ in vv. 4–19:**
- Matthew Henry sees Gethsemane and Calvary in these verses, and Christ's resurrection in the rescue. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-10.htm
- Guzik lists vv. 1–6 as pointing to Jesus' death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/

## Verses 20–25: "according to my righteousness"

This is where commentators disagree most. The big question is how David could claim righteousness when he later sinned with Bathsheba.

**How the traditions handle it:**
- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill says David's own works can earn nothing from God. The verse must mean the justice of David's cause, especially that he didn't kill Saul. He also applies it fully to Christ's righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-20.htm
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon says that before God David was a humble sinner. But against the people slandering him, he could truly claim clean hands, a righteousness given by grace. He also notes the verses are easily understood as spoken by the Messiah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps018.cfm
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin says God's reward is a matter of free grace, not merit, because even our good works need pardon. He says there is a particular reason David speaks this way here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-20.html
- **Wesleyan/Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke focuses on how David treated Saul. David was Saul's friend and acted rightly toward him while Saul acted wrongly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-20.html
- **Messianic reading:** A commentary on BibleHub quotes Dr. Horne. He limits David's claim to his loyalty to true worship or his innocence of false charges, and suggests the passage is better read as spoken by Christ. The same commentary adds that most interpreters think David speaks for himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-20.htm
- **Evangelical (Constable):** Constable says David isn't claiming to have earned God's favour. He is showing that God kept his covenant promises (Deuteronomy 28). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-20.html
- **Pentecostal/charismatic (Guzik):** Guzik says David refused to take Saul's throne by violence or scheming, and God rewarded that with a throne no one could take from him. After his repentance, David never fell in the same way again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-18/

**v. 20:**
- Pulpit says David doesn't mean he was completely blameless. He means honest purpose and a good conscience (1 Peter 3:21). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Cambridge Bible notes the verb can just mean "dealt with me." It says this isn't boasting but a testimony to God's faithfulness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-20.htm

**v. 21:**
- Pulpit says the word for "wickedly departed" means wilful, persistent wickedness. David never uses it of himself, not even in his psalms of repentance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Spurgeon says God never leaves his people, so they should be careful not to leave him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-20.htm

**v. 22:**
- Pulpit: the wicked throw God's commands behind their backs, but David kept them in front of him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 23:**
- Pulpit: "my iniquity" means the particular sin David was most tempted by (compare Hebrews 12:1). We can't tell what it was. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Benson, following Bishop Patrick, says David refused to copy his enemies' wrongdoing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-20.htm
- Utley says the passage isn't a claim to be sinless. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-18

**v. 24:**
- Pulpit: verse 24 repeats verse 20 for emphasis. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- Utley calls vv. 20 and 24 an *inclusio*, a pair of matching lines that frame a section. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-18
- Matthew Poole: because David wouldn't save himself by killing Saul, God rescued him in a better way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-20.htm

**v. 25:**
- Pulpit: the rule is that God treats people the way they treat him. The word for "faithful" (*chasid*) means kind and loving. It quotes the *Speaker's Commentary*: God responds to the good in kind, but can't himself be crooked toward the wicked (v. 26). He can only oppose them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

## Modern scholarship (from older and evangelical sites)
- **v. 1 and 2 Samuel 22:** Pulpit says v. 1 was left out of the 2 Samuel version as too private for public worship. Utley reports a lexicon (BDB) view that it may have been added later. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html and https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-18
- **v. 10:** Ellicott says the idea of winged attendants grew from storm clouds, possibly shaped by Assyrian art. He mentions a suggestion to read "chariot" instead of "cherub." He also says the 2 Samuel reading "was seen" is a copying error. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-10.htm
